If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $y$-component of $F=⟨0,\,2y\sqrt{25-{x}^{2}-{z}^{2}},\,0⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral side of $S$ is parallel to the $y$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the left and right sides. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14079020/assets/320e0c3333aa59f4e856d7d869d6fece09b178ac1abb3acd402621977df9b496.png)

Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the right surface. On this surface, we have $y=3$ for ${x}^{2}+{z}^{2}\le 9.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $y=3$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨0,\,2y\sqrt{25-{x}^{2}-{z}^{2}},\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,2(3)\sqrt{25-{x}^{2}-{z}^{2}},\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,6\sqrt{25-{x}^{2}-{z}^{2}},\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩ \\  & =6\sqrt{25-{x}^{2}-{z}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{1}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}6\sqrt{25-{x}^{2}-{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}S \\  & =6{∬}_{D}\sqrt{25-{x}^{2}-{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying a change of variables $(x,z)\to (r,\theta ),\text{d}A=r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}6{∬}_{D}\sqrt{25-{x}^{2}-{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & =6{∬}_{D}\sqrt{25-{r}^{2}}\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =6{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}r\sqrt{25-{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =6{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{0}^{3}r\sqrt{25-{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r \\  & =6\cdot 2\pi \cdot {[-\frac{1}{3}{(25-{r}^{2})}^{3/2}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =-4\pi (64-125) \\  & =-4\pi (-61) \\  & =244\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the left surface. On this surface, we have $y=0$ for ${x}^{2}+{z}^{2}\le 9.$ Therefore, for everywhere on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
F(x,0,z)=⟨0,\,2(0)\sqrt{25-{x}^{2}-{z}^{2}},\,0⟩=⟨0,\,0,\,0⟩.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}0\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}0\,\text{d}S \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =244\pi +0 \\  & =244\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that only the y-component of F=⟨0,2y25−x2−z2,0⟩ is non-zero. Since the lateral side of S is parallel to the y-axis, the flux of F through S will be non-zero only at the left and right sides.


Let's consider the flux of F through these two sides.

  • Let S1 denote the right surface. On this surface, we have y=3 for x2+z2≤9. The outward-pointing unit normal vector to S1 is n1=⟨0,1,0⟩. Using the fact that y=3 on S1, we have F⋅n1=⟨0,2y25−x2−z2,0⟩⋅⟨0,1,0⟩=⟨0,2(3)25−x2−z2,0⟩⋅⟨0,1,0⟩=⟨0,625−x2−z2,0⟩⋅⟨0,1,0⟩=625−x2−z2. Therefore, the flux of F across S1 is given by ∬S1F⋅dS=∬S1F⋅n1dS=∬S1625−x2−z2dS=6∬D25−x2−z2dA. Applying a change of variables (x,z)→(r,θ),dA=rdrdθ, we have 6∬D25−x2−z2dA=6∬D25−r2⋅rdrdθ=6∫02π∫03r25−r2drdθ=6∫02πdθ∫03r25−r2dr=6⋅2π⋅[−13(25−r2)3/2]03=−4π(64−125)=−4π(−61)=244π.

  • Let S2 denote the left surface. On this surface, we have y=0 for x2+z2≤9. Therefore, for everywhere on S2, we have F(x,0,z)=⟨0,2(0)25−x2−z2,0⟩=⟨0,0,0⟩. Therefore, ∬S2F⋅ndS=∬S20⋅ndS=∬S20dS=0.

Finally, ∬SF⋅dS=∬SF⋅ndS=∬S1F⋅ndS+∬S2F⋅ndS=244π+0=244π.
